title: Theoretical Foundations of Computer Science
summary: What machines can compute and how fast: finite automata and regular languages, context-free grammars and pushdown automata, Turing machines and the limits of decidability, and the classes P, NP and NP-complete. The course follows Sipser's Introduction to the Theory of Computation closely and is taught as a flipped classroom: you read and watch at home, and lectures are used for questions and quizzes. Optional weekly lab assignments are peer reviewed, and one closed-book written exam gives the whole grade.

basis.description: The archive lists 17 lectures of CSE2315 Automata, Computability and Complexity by number only, with no slide text. Time shares count lectures per topic, placed by the weekly lab assignments and Acing ACC sessions (two lectures a week); the last two lectures were exam preparation and are left out.
basis.caveat: The lecture-to-topic split is an estimate: only the weekly schedule and lab topics show what each lecture covered, and the three one-lecture topics may have shared slots. The material is from CSE2315 in quarter 3; from 2026-27 the course is CSE22B in year 2, quarter 2, with the same three parts, so the schedule may differ.

topics.name: DFAs, NFAs and closure properties
know: The formal definition of a DFA as a [[5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F)]], the extended transition function and what it means to accept a word
NFAs with epsilon transitions, and why a transition diagram of an NFA cannot always be written as a DFA 5-tuple
The subset construction from Sipser for turning an NFA into a DFA, including epsilon closures and leaving out unreachable states
The product construction for union and intersection, and how to adapt it for difference or XOR
Closure of regular languages under [[union, concatenation, star, complement, intersection, difference and reversal]], with the NFA constructions for union, concatenation and star
Why [[swapping accept and non-accept states complements a DFA but not an NFA]]
do: Design a DFA or NFA for a described language within a given number of states
Convert an NFA to a DFA with the Sipser procedure and name the states as sets
Build a DFA for the intersection, union, difference or XOR of two DFAs
Decide whether a modified automaton model (one accept state, a different acceptance rule) recognises exactly the regular languages, and argue both directions
pitfalls: Forgetting the [[epsilon closure of the start state or of each target set]] in the subset construction
Handing in a result of the subset construction that is still not a valid DFA, for example with a missing transition on some symbol
Complementing an NFA by flipping its accept states

topics.name: Regular expressions and GNFAs
know: The inductive definition of regular expressions with union, concatenation and star, and the empty set versus the empty word
The equivalence of regular expressions and finite automata, and the constructions in both directions
The GNFA: [[one start state with no incoming edges, one accept state with no outgoing edges]], and a regular expression on every other pair of states
The state-ripping procedure from Sipser that turns a GNFA into a regular expression, and why the order of ripping changes the expression but not the language
do: Write a regular expression for a described language, such as all words whose third-to-last symbol is an a
Turn an NFA into a GNFA and rip out a given state, writing the new edge labels
Read a GNFA or regular expression and describe its language in plain English
pitfalls: Forgetting to add the new start and accept states with epsilon edges before ripping states
Dropping the self-loop of the ripped state from the new edge labels

topics.name: Pumping lemma and non-regularity
know: The exact statement of the pumping lemma for regular languages: pumping length p, split [[w = xyz with |y| > 0 and |xy| <= p, and xy^i z in L for all i >= 0]]
The proof-by-contradiction template: [[suppose L is regular, pick a word of length at least p that is in L, cover every allowed split, find an i that leaves L]]
Why the choice of word decides whether the proof can be finished, and what makes a word unsuitable
How to prove a language is regular instead, by giving a DFA, NFA or regular expression or using closure properties
do: Judge whether a started pumping-lemma proof with a given word can be finished, and finish it or explain why not
Choose a good word for languages with counting conditions, such as a^n b^m with n <= m
Handle every case of the split, including i = 0 and the case where x is empty
pitfalls: Treating only one convenient split instead of all splits that the conditions |y| > 0 and |xy| <= p allow
Picking a word that is not in L or is shorter than p, or a word where pumping can stay inside L
Assuming every proof given on the exam can be finished: some started proofs use a word that does not work

topics.name: Context-free grammars and PDAs
know: Context-free grammars as a [[4-tuple (V, Sigma, R, S)]], derivations, leftmost derivations and parse trees
Ambiguity: [[a word with two different leftmost derivations or parse trees]], and the difference between an ambiguous word and an ambiguous grammar
Chomsky normal form and the Sipser conversion steps: [[new start variable, remove epsilon rules, remove unit rules, then split long rules and replace terminals]]
Pushdown automata: transitions of the form a, x -> y, the bottom-of-stack marker $, and nondeterminism
The equivalence of CFGs and PDAs, and closure of context-free languages under union, concatenation and star
do: Write a grammar for a described language within a limit on rules or variables
Convert a grammar to Chomsky normal form with the Sipser procedure, showing every step
Prove a grammar is ambiguous by giving two derivations of one word
Design a PDA within a given number of states, or describe the language of a given PDA in set-builder notation
Build grammars for the union, concatenation or star of given grammars
pitfalls: Skipping intermediate steps of the CNF conversion when the question asks for them
Not adding a new start variable first, so the start variable still appears on a right-hand side
Reading past how $ is pushed and popped in a given PDA, and so describing the wrong language

topics.name: Turing machines and their variants
know: The Turing machine as a [[7-tuple with input alphabet Sigma, tape alphabet Gamma (which contains the blank)]], and separate accept and reject states
Configurations, such as u q v, and how a computation moves from one configuration to the next on a tape bounded on the left
Recognisers versus deciders: [[a machine can loop on some words and still have a decidable language]]
Variants that are equally powerful: multitape, nondeterministic TMs and enumerators, and how a DTM simulates an NTM
The Church-Turing thesis and the level of detail of a high-level description
do: Trace a given TM on a word as a sequence of configurations, and find a word on which it loops
Draw a TM within a given number of states for a simple language
Explain whether a given TM is a decider and whether its language is decidable
Give a high-level description of an enumerator, or show that a new machine model is as powerful as a TM
pitfalls: Confusing whether M is a decider with whether L(M) is decidable
Forgetting that [[the tape is bounded on the left]] unless the question says otherwise

topics.name: Decidability and reductions
know: Decidable, Turing-recognisable and co-Turing-recognisable languages, and the theorem that [[a language is decidable if and only if it is both recognisable and co-recognisable]]
The decidable problems about automata and grammars, such as [[A_DFA, E_DFA, EQ_DFA, A_CFG and E_CFG]]
[[Undecidability of A_TM]] by diagonalisation, and the undecidable problems [[HALT_TM, E_TM and EQ_TM]]
Proof by reduction: assume a decider R for L and build a decider S for A_TM, which gives a contradiction
Mapping reductions A <=m B: [[a computable f with w in A if and only if f(w) in B]], and what they carry over in each direction
Dovetailing to show recognisability when a machine has to run on many inputs, and Rice's theorem as a shortcut for properties of TM languages
do: Prove that a language about TMs is recognisable or co-recognisable, usually by dovetailing
Prove that such a language is undecidable by a reduction from A_TM, HALT_TM, E_TM or EQ_TM
Prove that it is not recognisable, using that it is co-recognisable but undecidable
Complete a given mapping reduction by saying what the constructed machine must accept, and state what it proves
Prove or refute claims that combine reductions, subsets and decidability
pitfalls: Reducing in the wrong direction, from L to the undecidable problem instead of [[from the undecidable problem to L]]; the rubric deducts a point and grades the rest as if that direction were meant
Writing a decider that runs a TM directly where it can loop, instead of dovetailing
Concluding from a reduction to a decidable problem that the language is undecidable, or from subset relations that decidability carries over

topics.name: P, NP and NP-completeness
know: Time complexity on a single-tape deterministic TM, the classes TIME(t(n)), P, NP and EXP, and why the machine model matters for TIME
NP as the problems with a [[polynomial-time verifier for a certificate]], and its equivalence to nondeterministic polynomial time
Karp reductions A <=P B, NP-hard and NP-complete, and that NP is closed downwards under them
The Cook-Levin theorem and the standard NP-complete problems: [[SAT, 3SAT, Clique, Vertex Cover, Hamiltonian path and cycle, Subset Sum]]
The standing exam assumption that [[P is not NP and NP is not EXP]], and what each claim would mean if P = NP
do: Prove that a problem is in NP: [[name the certificate, list the checks and give a polynomial bound for each]]
Give a small yes-instance or no-instance of 3SAT, Vertex Cover or HAMC with set sizes
Apply a given reduction to your instance, show it breaks, and repair one step of it
Use a polynomial-time decider for a decision problem to find an actual solution, and give the running time
Prove or refute claims that chain Karp and mapping reductions between P, NP, NP-hard and NPC
pitfalls: Leaving out the time complexity of the verifier's checks when proving membership in NP
Arguing that a fast algorithm in Java puts a problem in TIME(n^2), forgetting the cost of simulating it on a single-tape DTM
Applying a reduction carelessly to your own instance, so the result does not show the flaw

prerequisites: Proof techniques from Reasoning and Logic: contradiction, contraposition, induction and quantifiers
Sets, functions, relations and countability, with confident set-builder notation
Big-O notation and the running time of simple algorithms
Graph basics and standard graph problems from Algorithms and Data Structures: paths, cycles, spanning trees, shortest paths
practical: Optional lab assignments, one a week (eight in 2024-25), made of exam-level questions, often old exam questions. You may work alone or in a pair, hand in a paper copy at a peer review session, mark each other's work and then get feedback from a TA in a booked slot. They do not count towards the grade. Weekly Acing ACC sessions each pose one harder goal problem, broken into guiding questions.
studyAdvice: Read the Sipser sections before each lecture: the lectures assume you have, and the exam requires the book's procedures by name
Do every weekly lab assignment and compare with the solutions; they are exam questions in all but name
Drill the fixed procedures until they are mechanical: subset construction, product construction, GNFA ripping, CNF conversion
Learn the proof templates as fixed structures: pumping lemma, recognisable by dovetailing, undecidable by reduction from A_TM, in NP by verifier
Give the second half at least as much time as the first: decidability and complexity carry about half of the exam points
Practise true-or-false claims about reductions and classes, starting each answer with the verdict and a counterexample where false
Fill your hand-written A4 sheet with the definitions, the closure and decidability tables and the reduction directions
